note: Nonsteroidal MRAs (finerenone; esaxerenone and apararenone in Japan) were built on the uninephrectomised DOCA-salt rat, where equinatriuretic dosing against eplerenone was used to claim kidney protection with less hyperkalaemia; ARTS-DN (2015) and FIDELIO-DKD (2020) were the patient tests.
label: Diabetic kidney disease (nonsteroidal MRA)

engagement.model: Rat natriuresis (urinary Na/K) after MR-agonist challenge
engagement.note: Rat natriuresis (urinary Na/K) was the engagement read-out; finerenone was 3-10x eplerenone's natriuretic potency and efficacy was compared at equinatriuretic doses.
engagement.quote: Finerenone reduced cardiac hypertrophy, plasma prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide, and proteinuria more efficiently than eplerenone when comparing equinatriuretic doses.
engagement.judgement: Abstract only (J Cardiovasc Pharmacol, paywalled). Barfacker 2012 (10.1002/cmdc.201200081) is MeSH-indexed Rats/Sodium/Potassium and probably holds earlier rat natriuresis data, but its abstract does not say so, so the strip opens 2014.

engagement.model: Rat natriuresis (urinary Na/K) after MR-agonist challenge
engagement.note: Healthy men under fludrocortisone: 20 mg finerenone out-natriuresed 50 mg eplerenone (Bayer Study 13786, NCT01473108), the potency ranking the rat gave.
engagement.short: Finerenone out-natriuresed eplerenone in healthy men
engagement.quote: 20 mg of finerenone in either the PEG solution or as 2 x 10-mg tablets was more effective in increasing natriuresis compared to eplerenone administered as a 50-mg dose.
engagement.reason: Natriuresis ranking vs eplerenone held in humans
engagement.judgement: Healthy volunteers, not DKD patients. The FDA integrated review holds both the rat result (natriuresis at 0.3 mg/kg, 3- to 10-fold more potent than eplerenone) and Study 13786 but never sets them side by side; a 20 mg vs 50 mg dose comparison gives direction, not a potency ratio. Study 13786 was never published and has no posted registry results.

dose.note: Rat minimum effective dose was 1 mg/kg; human 10/20 mg came from ARTS-DN UACR saturation, with no published rat-to-human exposure comparison.
dose.short: Human dose set by UACR, not rat
dose.quote: In rats that developed chronic heart failure after coronary artery ligation, finerenone (1 mg·kg·d), but not eplerenone (100 mg·kg·d) improved systolic and diastolic left ventricular function and reduced plasma prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide levels.
dose.judgement: FDA review: kidney parameters and pro-fibrotic gene expression 'all responded significantly at 1 mg/kg' in the DOCA-salt rat, and 'effects of finerenone were largely saturated at 20 mg' by dose-exposure-response modelling of ARTS-DN. Nothing published relates the rat exposure at 1 mg/kg to the 20 mg human exposure, so untested rather than stretched.

efficacy.note: Uninephrectomised DOCA-salt rats on finerenone had less proteinuria, kidney and heart weight and pro-fibrotic gene expression than equinatriuretic eplerenone.
efficacy.short: DOCA-salt rat: less proteinuria and fibrosis
efficacy.quote: Finerenone treatment prevented deoxycorticosterone acetate-/salt-challenged rats from functional as well as structural heart and kidney damage at dosages not reducing systemic blood pressure.
efficacy.judgement: Hypertensive, not diabetic, kidney injury; the FDA review names this DOCA-salt/uninephrectomy rat (plus SHRSP and post-MI rat) as the filed pharmacology, so it is the model the class relied on. No diabetic rodent finerenone study predates FIDELIO in what I found.

efficacy.note: ARTS-DN: UACR fell dose-dependently (placebo-corrected ratio 0.62 at 20 mg), the clinical analogue of rat proteinuria; FIDELIO 2020 added CKD-progression HR 0.82.
efficacy.quote: Finerenone demonstrated a dose-dependent reduction in UACR.
efficacy.reason: Rat proteinuria drop held in patients
efficacy.judgement: Juxtaposed: the JAMA paper does not cite the rat. Outcome confirmation came with FIDELIO-DKD (Bakris 2020, 10.1056/NEJMoa2025845, HR 0.82; registry results 2021-07-19) and FIGARO-DKD (Pitt 2021, 10.1056/NEJMoa2110956; 2022-04-15). Second drug of the class: esaxerenone, DOCA-salt and Dahl rats (Arai 2015/2016) to ESAX-DN UACR remission 22% vs 4% (Ito 2020, 10.2215/CJN.06870520). Not 'neg': no nonsteroidal MRA failed in DKD.

safety.note: Rat work claimed organ protection 'with a reduced risk of electrolyte disturbances' versus steroidal MRAs; FDA-reviewed 6-month rat toxicology still showed serum potassium rising.
safety.short: Rat claims less hyperkalaemia than steroidal
safety.quote: We conclude that finerenone may offer end-organ protection with a reduced risk of electrolyte disturbances.
safety.judgement: The claim is relative to steroidal MRAs at equinatriuretic doses, not an absence of hyperkalaemia. FDA review: healthy dogs showed no plasma potassium change short-term, but in the 6-month rat study potassium 'was increased in females ... starting at the low dose of 0.5 mg/kg on day 179'.

safety.note: Rat potassium rise held: FIDELIO-DKD hyperkalaemia 21.4% vs 9.2% (discontinuation 2.3% vs 0.9%); FDA ties finerenone's pharmacology to lower hyperkalaemia than steroidal MRAs.
safety.short: Potassium rose in rat; hyperkalaemia doubled in DKD
safety.quote: Clinical data available to date also support that the structural and pharmacological differences between finerenone and steroidal MRAs have clinical relevance in reducing adverse events such as hyperkalemia and sexual side-effects.
safety.reason: Potassium rise predicted; hyperkalaemia real, managed
safety.judgement: Could be scored 'contra' if the rat is read as promising no hyperkalaemia: finerenone doubled hyperkalaemia vs placebo in FIDELIO-DKD (Agarwal 2022, 10.1681/ASN.2021070942: 21.4% vs 9.2% >5.5 mmol/L; NEJM: discontinuation 2.3% vs 0.9%). I scored 'same' because Kolkhof 2014 claimed only a reduced risk vs steroidal MRAs, the FDA-reviewed rat toxicology did flag rising potassium, and the FDA review itself links the pharmacology to lower clinical hyperkalaemia. The vs-steroidal claim has only been tested head-to-head in HFrEF+CKD (ARTS, Pitt 2013, 10.1093/eurheartj/eht187: 5.3% vs 12.7% on spironolactone), never in DKD. Esaxerenone caveat not scored: Dahl rats showed 'no hyperkalemia (>5.5mEq/L)' (Arai 2015, 10.1016/j.ejphar.2015.11.028) while ESAX-DN had 9% vs 2% with K >=5.5/6.0 mEq/L; no source compares the two. The FDA review's linking sentence is at class/pharmacology level, not a numeric rat-vs-FIDELIO potassium comparison.
